summary: Gravity in a Bottle addresses the challenge of making the history of humanity's silent, off-world spacecraft engaging and accessible, which currently makes it difficult for students and space enthusiasts to connect emotionally with archival mission data. To solve this, we created an interactive, story-driven web game set aboard the stranded vessel Odyssey-6, allowing players to explore an offline archive of real hardware left on Mercury, Venus, the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn through six tailored mini-games. By integrating official NASA mission archives, planetary imagery, and international space records—featuring iconic spacecraft like Ingenuity, Galileo, Lunokhod, and Venera—into an interactive web experience, our platform transforms technical space history into an emotional journey where restoring lost machines unlocks the signal home to Earth. Ultimately, Gravity in a Bottle empowers learners and space fans to discover the legacy of deep-space pioneers and see that no explorer is ever truly forgotten.
details:
Overview


Gravity in a Bottle is a retro sci-fi narrative and simulation web game set aboard the stranded spacecraft Odyssey-6. After 19 days without contact from Earth, the crew explores an interactive Solar System map, reads planetary dossiers on abandoned hardware, and plays 7 multi-stage historical probe simulations (Huygens, Lunokhod 1, Surveyor 3, Galileo, Ingenuity, Venera 13, and MESSENGER). Completing missions unlocks real NASA/ESA telemetry and a domain-locked Archive AI Q&A terminal until the crew restores Earth contact.

Benefits

  • Active Learning: Players experience real planetary physics and engineering limits (e.g., Venus's 465 °C heat, Mars's 1% air density, and 2.6-second lunar rover radio delays) instead of passively reading facts.
  • Instant Accessibility: Runs directly in any browser with zero installation and automatic local progress saving.

Intended Impact

We aim to reframe space exploration around human ingenuity and legacy, showing how silent probes and rovers left across the Solar System are enduring monuments to curiosity, and inspiring players through the engineering resilience behind them.


Technological Stack

  • Languages & Frameworks: TypeScript, React, Next.js, HTML5, CSS3, and Tailwind CSS.
  • AI & Audio: Google Gemini API (gemini-2.5-flash via @google/genai) for the in-character Archive Q&A bot, and the Web Audio API for procedural 8-bit sound effects.
  • Media & Hosting: Custom pixel-art sprites, NASA/ESA archival photography, Git/GitHub, and Vercel. Further credits are provided in the github repo and website.

Creative Exploration

  • Physics-Driven Minigames: We tried to ensure every simulation mirrors its real mission's unique failure modes, wrapped in a cohesive 16-bit CRT terminal aesthetic with pixel portraits and procedural audio- in a simplified, easy to grasp format.
  • History as a Survival Manual: We developed a short story where the crew "reverse-engineers" past probes' survival and communication tricks to repair their own backup dish.

Factors We Considered

  • Scientific Accuracy: Real mission dates, crush depths, thermal limits, and untouched flyby-only worlds (Uranus and Neptune).
  • Usability & Responsiveness: Multi-device sprite scaling, uncropped archival image carousels, and strict AI guardrails so the chatbot stays accurate and in character.
  • Generative AI Usage: Leveraged the capabilities of genAI in various stages of development, both code and assets, to realize the large scope of the project within the hackathon's limited timeframe.

projectRefs: recorded most distant landing from Earth

Launched aboard the Soviet Union's Luna 17 spacecraft in November 1970, it dramatically outlived its planned 90-day mission timeline to operate for 11 lunar days (322 Earth days). While its electronics officially failed on October 4, 1971, its French-supplied laser retroreflector array remains fully operational today. Physicists continue to shoot lasers from ground observatories straight at the parked rover to map the Moon's distance within centimeters.

While its electronics officially failed on October 4, 1971, its French-supplied laser retroreflector array remains fully operational today. Physicists continue to shoot lasers from ground observatories straight at the parked rover to map the Moon's distance within centimeters.

Driving it was incredibly difficult because its television cameras sent only one single image frame back to Earth every 20 seconds. Operators had to navigate a slow-motion slideshow, and the rover included a unique 9th trailing odometer wheel designed strictly to measure exactly how much the main 8 wheels were spinning and slipping in the loose lunar soil.
Parked at the Mare Imbrium (Sea of Rains) region of the Moon.

It was a one-way mission. The rover relied on solar power by day and a Polonium-210 radioisotope heater to survive freezing two-week nights. It finally ceased operations on October 4, 1971, after vastly outlasting its 3-month design life.

Deep-Space X-Ray Background: Equipped with an X-ray telescope, it functioned as the first lunar astronomical observatory. Free from the distortion of Earth's atmosphere, it discovered the precise baseline levels of cosmic X-ray background radiation streaming through the universe
